findings.summary: crates/athena-core/src/store.rs is not among the reading's deliverables
findings.evidence: A change outside the listed deliverables widens the scope.

findings.summary: crates/athena-cli/src/display.rs is not among the reading's deliverables
findings.evidence: A change outside the listed deliverables widens the scope.

findings.summary: Measured minutes after a cited change can rest on a single landed job.
findings.evidence: The plan says the measured value is the 'window median of landed jobs landing after the cited job, capped at the newest 10, needing at least 1'. One job's span is noise, and the recorded predicted-versus-measured result would treat it as the change's effect. Fix: Require a minimum sample before writing a follow-up, for example 5 landed jobs, which is half the cadence (name it as a const). Until then, defer the follow-up to a later review. Record the sample size in the follow-up and test the deferral.

findings.summary: The landing tail also counts time a merged pull request waits for a person or for CI. That inflates the stage the model is asked to fix.
findings.evidence: The tail is outcome.at (later_outcome first) minus the end of the last invocation. A job that waited on a blocked or human merge shows that wait as 'landing and rebuild', so the model may blame landing for time spent waiting on a person. Fix: Keep the single stage, but have the text() label and the hestia.md section say that it includes merge and CI waits. Also give the model the count of jobs that had a later_outcome (blocked, then landed) so it can tell the two apart.

findings.summary: A cited change is found only when a later request's text contains the review record id. That depends on authors following an instruction.
findings.evidence: The request body asks authors to cite the id. A pipeline change made in response but written without the id is never compared, so the follow-up quietly records nothing. Fix: Also count jobs whose text names the design request's job id (dependencies are already written as job ids in the request format). Say in hestia.md that uncited changes get no follow-up.

summary: I checked the plan's claims against the snapshot and they hold. `review_passes` (hestia.rs:904) is the housekeeping entry point and returns summary lines. `StewardRequest::new` is the shared builder used in hestia.rs and code_health.rs. `structural_pass_open` (code_health.rs:535) is the marker-based duplicate check the plan copies. `REVIEW_EVERY = 10` is at code_health.rs:46. `Records` keeps one typed Vec per record kind with a load arm (store.rs:251/318/354), so the store.rs edit is really needed. Status text is printed by hand in display.rs (the `check_durations` block is at line 1033), so the display.rs edit is needed for the section to appear in `athena status`. `JobRecords.later_outcome` exists. Invocations carry `started_at`/`ended_at`, and `Role` has Reader, Planner and Critic. steward, auditor and audience all use `models.verifier` through `agent_spec`/`invoke_and_record`. `FakeAgentDriver::new(script)` exists. Every demonstration goes through production entry points (`Throughput::compute`, `Athena::throughput_review`, `check_record_file`) with exact-number or count assertions, and each would fail without the behavior. The fake driver only returns canned JSON. The design is sound: one records-based median shared by status and the trigger, a durable review record for cadence and the prediction, and duplicate suppression by marker as the code-health pass already does. Athena's own two scope findings are answered by the stated need for each file. What remains is minor: the measured-saving sample size, possible confusion inside the landing tail, and how cited changes are found.
